source.title: Stochastic Training is Not Necessary for Generalization
source.authors: Jonas Geiping; Micah Goldblum; Phillip E. Pope; Michael Möller; T. Goldstein

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper, including appendices; no material truncation or garbling noted.
record.tranche_reason: It compares full-batch gradient descent with mini-batch SGD on held-out CIFAR-10 accuracy, using different training recipes and measures than the claim’s cited studies.
record.gate_note: The study tests whether full-batch training has worse held-out performance and whether training changes can close that gap. Its main comparison changes both batch size and recipe: the baseline uses 300 epochs, while adapted full-batch runs use 3000. The study does not test random-label memorization, width scaling, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, adaptive optimizers, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples. Cited prior-work results are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares mini-batch and full-batch held-out accuracy on CIFAR-10. It tests V5's fixed-epoch penalty and its allowance for recovery through longer training and recipe changes. It is not an original source for V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that full-batch training can match strong CIFAR-10 SGD performance using longer training, clipping and explicit gradient regularization, including a deterministic setting with fixed augmented data. They argue that stochastic mini-batching and its gradient noise are not necessary for strong generalization in these examples, while emphasizing much greater computational cost. They do not rule out chaotic dynamics or stochastic mathematical descriptions of deterministic GD.
record.recipe_differences: The full-batch method uses full-dataset gradients and, for its strongest results, 10 times as many epochs as the SGD baseline, gradient clipping, explicit gradient regularization and sometimes smaller accumulation blocks or shuffling. The study is a paper, not a repository.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with training duration, gradient clipping, explicit gradient regularization, regularizer accumulation block size, shuffling, data augmentation, model architecture and learning rate. VGG-16 required a larger clipping value.

fits_no_version.finding: Strong CIFAR-10 accuracy is attainable without stochastic mini-batching, reshuffling or resampled augmentation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stochastic gradient noise is not necessary for strong image-classification generalization when deterministic explicit regularization and substantially greater computation are allowed.

fits_no_version.finding: Random-direction landscape visualizations become qualitatively flatter after clipping and gradient regularization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In these training interventions, improved validation accuracy accompanies qualitatively flatter loss landscapes; this does not establish V7's magnitude-aware ranking of generalization gaps.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2022; text notes this is the uncompressed version of the final paper presented at ICLR 2022)
record.problems: The main baseline and strongest full-batch comparison use different epoch counts (300 versus 3000), so the study does not isolate batch size under a fixed epoch budget for its adapted recipe. Scope is CIFAR-10 vision models. Several reported values have no standard deviation and are single runs; the authors also state that in a few edge cases they report maximal validation accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 gradient-noise variants and Appendix Tables 5–8 include auxiliary measures, ablations and numerical-stability checks; not extracted because they are not necessary to represent the main batch-size and recipe comparisons for V5. The no-augmentation and fixed-dataset results are included in R36–R40.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width scaling beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under the specified tuning regimes.

Language models, other datasets, the workload-dependent batch-size threshold, and successful recovery at the small-batch baseline's fixed epoch budget. Strong recovery here uses longer training and several simultaneous changes.
Dropout effects and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness ranking generalization gaps and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples versus matched random removal.

missing.what: On fixed 10× CIFAR-10, full-batch longer training without clipping or gradient regularization reaches 88.44% in a single run, versus 95.11% with the strong recipe and 95.20% for SGD. This main-table result shows that duration and schedule changes alone do not recover parity.

record.verdict_notes: All rows bear on V5, including its explicit recovery clause; successful adaptation therefore supports that version rather than automatically limiting it. Comparator rows remain linked but do not independently demonstrate an effect. The auxiliary Tables 5–8 are expressly declared in rows_left_out, so their omitted results are not listed as missing. Table 5 nevertheless clarifies interpretation: baseline full-batch training has training loss 0.521 versus SGD's 0.0017, whereas clipped full-batch training reaches 0.00173 and still has lower validation accuracy. No fixed-budget recovery or formal significance of the small VGG residual differences is established.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Widening one-hidden-layer networks beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and the effects of their tuning.

Language models and fixed-epoch comparisons for the adapted full-batch recipes; the study primarily compares CIFAR-10 image classifiers, and its strongest full-batch recipes use more epochs than the SGD baseline.
Dropout and its interaction with training-set size or data augmentation.
A magnitude-aware sharpness measure and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
